```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.8)
```

## A chart maps columns to visual properties

```{r}
#| label: template
#| eval: false
ggplot() +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = column1, y = column2), data = my_tibble)
```

- `ggplot()`: an empty chart. `+` adds layers.
- `geom_*()`: the **geometry** that draws the data: points, lines, bars.
- `mapping = aes()`: **mappings** from columns to visual properties: x, y, colour, size, fill.
- `data =`: the tibble to plot.

## A small dataset: Kerrisdale in 2017

```{r}
#| label: kerr17
library(tidyverse)
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")

kerr17 <- bca |>
  filter(neigh_label == "Kerrisdale", year(sale_date) == 2017) |>
  mutate(price_m = price / 1e6)
kerr17 |> select(floorarea, price_m, act_use_cat, bedrooms) |> head(4)
```

`kerr17` holds the `r nrow(kerr17)` sales in one Vancouver neighbourhood in one year: few enough to see every point. `price_m` is the price in millions of dollars.

## geom_point() shows a relationship {.nostretch}

```{r}
#| label: point
#| fig-height: 3.3
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(floorarea, price_m), data = kerr17)
```

R matches unnamed arguments by position. `aes()` takes `x` then `y`, and a `geom_*()` takes `mapping` first, so we drop those names. Keep `data =`: it comes second in a `geom_*()`.

::: {.notes}
- Swapping the order, `geom_point(kerr17, aes(...))`, fails with "`mapping` must be created by `aes()`. ✖ You've supplied a data frame."
:::

## Map more columns to colour and size

```{r}
#| label: colour-size
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(floorarea, price_m, colour = act_use_cat, size = bedrooms),
             data = kerr17)
```

## Mapping and setting are different

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: mapped
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.7
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(floorarea, price_m,
        colour = "blue"),
    data = kerr17)
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: set
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.7
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(floorarea, price_m),
    colour = "blue",
    data = kerr17)
```
:::
::::

Inside `aes()`, `"blue"` is a data value, as if every row held `"blue"`: ggplot2 maps it to a colour and adds a legend. Outside `aes()`, it sets the colour.

## alpha is a setting: it makes points see-through

```{r}
#| label: alpha
#| fig-height: 3.3
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(floorarea, price_m, colour = act_use_cat, size = bedrooms),
             alpha = 0.5, data = kerr17)
```

The chart from two slides back, with `alpha` set: 0 is invisible, 1 is solid.

## Quick check: what does this draw?

```{r}
#| label: quiz-setting
#| eval: false
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(floorarea, price_m), colour = act_use_cat, data = kerr17)
```

**A.** Points coloured by property type  **B.** An error

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: quiz-setting-answer
#| echo: false
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(floorarea, price_m), colour = act_use_cat, data = kerr17)
```

**B.** Outside `aes()`, R looks for an object named `act_use_cat`, not a column of `kerr17`. Columns go inside `aes()`.
:::

## Layers stack: lines and points

```{r}
#| label: lines
#| fig-height: 2.4
avg_price <- bca |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat), data = avg_price) +
  geom_point(aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat), data = avg_price)
```

Each layer has its own mapping and data, so we write both twice.

## Global and local mappings

```{r}
#| label: global
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(avg_price, aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```

The same chart as the last slide. Data and `aes()` in `ggplot()` are **global**: every layer uses them, so you write them once. `aes()` in a `geom_*()`, as on the last slide, is **local**: only that layer uses it.

::: {.notes}
- `ggplot()` takes the data first; a `geom_*()` takes the mapping first. A layer usually reuses the plot's data but needs its own mapping.
- Data first in `ggplot()` also lets you pipe into it: `kerr17 |> count(act_use_cat) |> ggplot(aes(n, act_use_cat))`.
:::

## geom_text() maps a column to text

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: text
#| eval: false
top8 <- kerr17 |>
  arrange(desc(price_m)) |>
  head(8) |>
  mutate(address = paste(str_no, str_name))

ggplot(kerr17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = address), data = top8)
```
:::

The text layer takes x and y from `ggplot()` but has its own `label` and `data`: `r nrow(kerr17)` rows, 8 labels. Each label sits on its point, so labels of close points run into each other.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| label: text-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.8
top8 <- kerr17 |>
  arrange(desc(price_m)) |>
  head(8) |>
  mutate(address = paste(str_no, str_name))

ggplot(kerr17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = address), data = top8)
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- `paste()` is `paste0()` with a space between the pieces.
- `nudge_y = 0.3` moves every label up by the same amount. It does not stop labels running into each other.
:::

## geom_text_repel() moves labels apart

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: text-repel
#| eval: false
library(ggrepel)

ggplot(kerr17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = address), data = top8)
```
:::

The ggrepel package adds geoms to ggplot2. Swap `geom_text()` for `geom_text_repel()` and keep the arguments: the labels move off each other and off the points they label.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| label: text-repel-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.8
library(ggrepel)

ggplot(kerr17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = address), data = top8)
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- ggrepel is in the deck 01 install list. Otherwise run `install.packages("ggrepel")` once in the Console.
- It avoids only the points in its own layer, `top8`. A label can still cover one of the other points.
- Label a few points, not all. With a label on every sale, ggrepel drops most of them and warns "unlabeled data points (too many overlaps)".
- If the labels move between runs, `seed = 1` keeps them in one place.
- `geom_label_repel()` draws each label in a box. A line joins a label to its point when the label moves far; `min.segment.length = 0` draws one for every label.
:::

## Choose the geometry for the question

| Question | Geometry |
|---|---|
| How are two numbers related? | `geom_point()` |
| How does a value change over time? | `geom_line()` |
| How do groups compare? | `geom_col()` for values you computed, `geom_bar()` to count rows |
| How is one number distributed? | `geom_histogram()` |
| Which points are which? | `geom_text()`, `geom_text_repel()` |

## geom_bar() counts for you; geom_col() does not

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: bar-count
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 1.8
ggplot(kerr17, aes(y = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_bar()
```
:::

The same chart. `geom_bar()` counts the rows itself, so its axis says `count`, a column it computed. `geom_col()` draws the `n` you computed.
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: count-table
kerr17 |>
  count(act_use_cat)
```

```{r}
#| label: col-count
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 1.8
kerr17 |>
  count(act_use_cat) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, act_use_cat)) +
  geom_col()
```
:::
:::
::::

## Some geoms compute what they draw

| Geom | Computes before drawing |
|---|---|
| `geom_bar()` | The number of rows in each group |
| `geom_histogram()` | Bins, then the number of rows in each bin |
| `geom_smooth()` | A fitted line |
| `geom_boxplot()` | The median and quartiles |
| `geom_col()`, `geom_point()`, `geom_line()` | Nothing: they draw the values as given |

::: {.key-point}
When a geom computes, ask what it computed. `geom_bar()` counts rows, not people (deck 10).
:::

::: {.notes}
- `geom_bar(stat = "identity")` is the same as `geom_col()`. AI-written and older code often uses it.
- `after_stat(count)`, or the older `..count..`, refers to a column the geom computed.
- `geom_bar(aes(x, y))` fails with "`stat_count()` must only have an x or y aesthetic": `geom_bar()` computes y itself.
:::

## Look up what a geom draws

| Resource | Use it to |
|---|---|
| [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html) ([PDF](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf)) | See every geom as a small picture |
| [ggplot2 reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/) | Read one function's arguments and example charts |
| [R Graph Gallery](https://r-graph-gallery.com/) | Find a chart type and see working code |
| [From Data to Viz](https://www.data-to-viz.com/) | Choose a chart from the kind of data you have |

In Positron, `?geom_histogram` opens the help page, and `example(geom_histogram)` draws its examples.

**Try it:** pick a geom from the cheat sheet that we have not used, read its page, and draw it with `kerr17`.
